A.explanation: From $V = IR$, $\text{A } \Omega$ does equal the volt, but $\Omega$ is a derived unit not an SI base unit.

B.explanation: From $P = VI$, $\text{W A}^{-1}$ does equal the volt, but $\text{W}$ is a derived unit not an SI base unit.

C.explanation: This has the correct $\text{kg m}^2 \text{ A}^{-1}$ part but the power of $\text{s}$ is $-1$ instead of $-3$.

D.explanation: Using $V = W/Q$ gives $\text{J C}^{-1} = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-2} / \text{A s} = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-3} \text{A}^{-1}$.

hints: Start from what a volt means in electricity: $V = W/Q$ or $V = P/I$, so the volt is joule per coulomb or watt per ampere.
Recall the base-unit forms: $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}$ for energy and $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$ for charge.
Divide the energy units by the charge units and combine the powers of $\text{s}$ to check whether $\text{s}^{-1}$ or $\text{s}^{-3}$ is needed.
walkthrough: Identify the defining relation for potential difference: $V = W/Q$, so $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$.
Express the joule in base units from work $W = Fs$: $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{m} = 1 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}$.
Express the coulomb in base units from charge $Q = It$: $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$.
Substitute: $1 \text{ V} = \frac{1 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}}{1 \text{ A s}} = 1 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{ s}^{-3} \text{ A}^{-1}$.
Options A and B still contain the derived units $\Omega$ and $\text{W}$, so they are not in base units, and option C has the wrong power of $\text{s}$. This is option D.
